# CHANGELOG sections are generated by git-cliff from Conventional Commits and commit footers, replacing the planned changelog fragments

## Context

CHANGELOG.md is written by hand. Commits edit `## [Unreleased]` directly and the release commit edits the entry again, so wording drifts between the docs and the changelog. [[research:modootoday/20261109150011]] planned an in-house scheme for 1.7.0 (C2–C5 in [[adr:modootoday/20261109141321]]): one fragment file per change under `changes/`, a check that user-facing commits ship one, and `script/changelog` plus `script/release-prep` to compile them.

The maintainer prefers a widely used tool to a home-grown one. The common GitHub tools differ in one way that matters here, because this repository pushes straight to `main` without pull requests ([[adr:modootoday/20261102203210]]):
- release-drafter reads merged pull request labels, so it has nothing to read here;
- release-please and the changesets bot work through a release pull request, which would need an exception to the direct-to-main rule;
- git-cliff generates the changelog from commit messages alone, has a maintained GitHub Action and needs no pull request.

The commits here already follow Conventional Commits.

## Decision

- **git-cliff generates the CHANGELOG's version sections.** A `cliff.toml` in the repository root maps commit types to the Keep a Changelog sections the lint expects:
  - `feat` goes to Added;
  - `fix` goes to Fixed;
  - `perf` and `refactor` with user impact go to Changed;
  - a `Deprecated:` footer goes to Deprecated;
  - `!` or a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer goes to Changed, with a breaking marker;
  - chores, CI, tests and internal docs are skipped unless a `Changelog:` footer says otherwise.
- **Commit footers carry what the subject cannot:**
  - `Changelog: <text>` replaces the subject in the entry, or `Changelog: none` leaves the commit out;
  - `Refs: adr:...` adds the ADR id;
  - `Visual: <text>` is collected into the release's `Visual:` line;
  - `Migration: <text>` feeds the Upgrade guide.
- **A commit-msg check enforces it.** A user-facing commit, one that touches shipped paths (`_layouts`, `_includes`, `_sass`, `assets`, `lib`, `exe`, `i18n`), has a Conventional Commit subject. If the subject alone would mislead, it also carries a `Changelog:` footer or `Changelog: none`. The check runs in the shared pre-push hook and in push CI, which checks the pushed range.
- **Release preparation uses git-cliff.**
  - `script/release-prep X.Y.Z` runs git-cliff for the new section.
  - It then writes the version, the install pins and `version-include`.
  - It leaves a one-paragraph hand-written summary at the top of the entry, which is the only hand-written part.
  - The release workflow builds the GitHub Release body from the same entry, through `script/release-notes`.
- **`## [Unreleased]` is generated** by `git-cliff --unreleased`. A test compares it with the committed file, so contributors stop editing it by hand.
- Entries released before this decision stay as written; the CHANGELOG lint keeps them unchanged against their tags.
- The C2–C5 fragment plan in adr:modootoday/20261109141321 is withdrawn; this record replaces it. C1, the lint, stays.

## Consequences

- One source for change notes: the commit that makes the change.
- A badly worded commit subject shows up in the changelog unless a `Changelog:` footer fixes it, so the commit-msg check and the release review are where wording is caught.
- git-cliff is a pinned dev dependency, the version-pinned GitHub Action or binary in CI and the release script. Nothing ships in the gem.
